**Form**: Individual Tax Return
**Section**: Income
**Question**: Eligible termination payment: assessable amount (other than excessive component)
**Label**: Taxable component of eligible termination payments below the reasonable benefit limit (RBL)
**General Notes**: The employee termination payment amount below the reasonable benefit limit.
**Latest or Current Conditions**: Latest year: 2006-07. This variable refers to an eligible termination payment (ETP), which includes: - a lump sum payment from your employer when the taxpayer retired or ceased employment - a lump sum payment from a superannuation fund, approved deposit fund, retirement savings account or life insurance company - a similar payment to those above, paid as the beneficiary of a person who has died. This is called a ‘death benefit ETP’. However, if the payments were made to the taxpayer as the trustee of a deceased estate they must be shown on the trust tax return, not on your personal tax return - a payment from the Tax Office of amounts collected from an employer either by way of Superannuation Guarantee Charge payments or payments to the Superannuation Holding Accounts Special Account. Lump sum payment from employer includes: - a payment in lieu of notice or a golden handshake - a payment for unused sick leave or unused rostered days off - compensation for loss of a job or wrongful dismissal - a redundancy payment or an approved early retirement scheme payment that exceeded the tax free threshold - a payment received because of invalidity - a similar payment paid to the trustee of a deceased estate after the death of an employee. An ETP also includes a payment from a superannuation fund, an approved deposit fund or a life insurance company such as: - payments, other than a pension or annuity, from a superannuation fund - payments received when a pension or annuity is changed into a lump sum - payments made to the trustee of a deceased estate. Lump sum payment received on termination of foreign employment and from a non-resident superannuation fund is recorded at item 19: Foreign source income and foreign assets or property (see isn_fsi_assessable_inc). The taxpayer may have the option to roll-over their ETP. This means transferring all or part of their ETP to a complying superannuation fund or an approved deposit fund or buying an annuity. This is not recorded under i_etp. A reasonable benefit limit (RBL) is the maximum amount of superannuation benefit that is taxed at concessional (or reduced) rates. Anything above the RBL is taxed at the marginal tax rate.

years of age, the rate under the threshold (see 1998 TaxPack) will be

the taxed element of the post-June 1983 component will be taxed at 20%
if the taxpayer is under 55 years of age. If the taxpayer is above 55
years of age, the rate under the threshold (see 1998 TaxPack) will be 0%
but above the threshold, the excess will be taxed at 15%.

payment (ETP), which includes:
- a lump sum payment from your employer when the taxpayer retired or
ceased employment
- a lump sum payment from a superannuation fund, approved deposit fund,
retirement savings account or life insurance company
- a similar payment to those above, paid as the beneficiary of a person
who has died. This is called a ‘death benefit ETP’. However, if the
payments were made to the taxpayer as the trustee of a deceased estate
they must be shown on the trust tax return, not on your personal tax
return
- a payment from the Tax Office of amounts collected from an employer
either by way of Superannuation Guarantee Charge payments or payments to
the Superannuation Holding Accounts Special Account.
Lump sum payment from employer includes:
- a payment in lieu of notice or a golden handshake
- a payment for unused sick leave or unused rostered days off
- compensation for loss of a job or wrongful dismissal
- a redundancy payment or an approved early retirement scheme payment
that exceeded the tax free threshold
- a payment received because of invalidity
- a similar payment paid to the trustee of a deceased estate after the
death of an employee.   An ETP also includes a payment from a
superannuation fund, an approved deposit fund or a life insurance
company such as:
- payments, other than a pension or annuity, from a superannuation
fund
- payments received when a pension or annuity is changed into a lump
sum
- payments made to the trustee of a deceased estate.

Lump sum payment received on termination of foreign employment and from
a non-resident superannuation fund is recorded at item 19: Foreign
source income and foreign assets or property (see
isn_fsi_assessable_inc).

The taxpayer may have the option to roll-over their ETP. This means
transferring all or part of their ETP to a complying superannuation fund
or an approved deposit fund or buying an annuity. This is not recorded
under i_etp.

A reasonable benefit limit (RBL) is the maximum amount of superannuation
benefit that is taxed at concessional (or reduced) rates. Anything above
the RBL is taxed at the marginal tax rate.

### i_div_frank
**Form**: Individual Tax Return
**Section**: Income
**Question**: Dividends: franked amount
**Label**: Income from dividends: franked amount
**General Notes**: Income from dividends: franked amount. Dividends paid to shareholders by Australian resident companies are taxed under a system known as ‘imputation’. It is called an imputation system because the tax paid by a company may be imputed or attributed to the shareholders. The tax paid by the company is allocated to shareholders by way of franking credits attached to the dividends they receive. The basis of the system is that if a company pays or credits you with dividends which have been franked, you may be entitled to a franking tax offset for the tax the company has paid on its income. The franking tax offset will cover or partly cover the tax payable on the dividends. Dividends can be fully franked (meaning that the whole amount of the dividend carries a franking credit) or partly franked (meaning that the dividend has a franked amount and an unfranked amount). The dividend statement or distribution statement you receive from the company paying the franked dividend must state the amount of the franking credit and the amounts of the franked and unfranked parts of the dividend. Franked dividends have a franking/imputation credit attached to them.
**Latest or Current Conditions**: This variable refers to franked amounts on dividends and distributions that were paid by Australian companies to taxpayers who owned shares. These include: - dividends applied under a dividend reinvestment plan - dividends that were dealt with on your behalf - bonus shares that qualify as dividends. Dividends include distributions by a corporate limited partnership or paid by a corporate unit trust, public trading trust, or listed investment company. They can also include: - earnings received, or were credited with, on a non-share equity interest - amounts received from, or were credited by, a private company as a shareholder or an associate of a shareholder in the form of payments, loans or debts forgiven (these are generally unfranked dividends) - amounts received from, or were credited by, the trustee of a trust estate in the form of payments, loans or debts forgiven where a private company in which they were a shareholder, or an associate of a shareholder, had an unpaid present entitlement (or was going to have such an entitlement by a certain time) from the trust (these are generally unfranked dividends). The dividend amounts recorded under this variable is the dividends that have a franking credit attached to them. Franking credits are amounts of tax paid by the company that are allocated to the taxpayer’s dividend or distributions. This franking credit can be claimed as a tax credit. However, taxpayer might not be entitled to claim the franking credits if: - within 45 days of buying the shares (90 days for certain preference shares), they either sold them or entered into an arrangement to reduce the risk of making a loss on them (Holding period rule) - they were under an obligation to make, or were likely to make, a related payment (Related payments rule), or - they received a dividend as a result of a dividend washing arrangement (Dividend washing integrity rule). If there are any shares in joint names, then only the proportion of dividends is shown. If the taxpayer: - received a distribution from a partnership or trust, see Supplement section question: Partnerships and trusts (is_pt_net_dist_pp or is_pt_net_dist_npp) (for example, in tax return form 2017-18, see question 13) - carried on a business of trading in shares and received income or loss, see Supplement section question: Net income or loss from business (is_bus_npp) (in tax return form 2017-18, see question 15) - sold, redeemed, cancelled or otherwise disposed of shares during the year (but did not carry on a business of trading in shares), see Supplement section question: Capital gains (is_cg_tot_current) (in tax return form 2017-18, see question 18) - received dividends from a foreign company, see Supplement section question: Foreign source income and foreign assets or property (is_fsi_other_foreign) (in tax return form 2017-18, see question 20) - received dividends from a New Zealand company with Australian franking credits attached, see Supplement section question: Foreign source income and foreign assets or property (is_frank_cr_nz_coy) (in tax return form 2017-18, see question 20) - received dividends or a distribution on which family trust distribution tax had been paid, see Supplement section question: Amount on which family trust distribution tax has been paid (as_family_trust_inc_txd) (in tax return form 2017-18, see question A5).
**Latest or Current Calculations**: Add up all franked dividend amounts from dividend statements. Do not include any TFN amounts.
**Earliest Conditions**: For 1990-91, the variable refers to franked amounts on dividends where the taxpayer was a shareholder in a company or held units in a corporate unit trust or a public trading trust. A corporate unit trusts are public trusts that are created as part of a reorganisation of a company. Public trading trusts are commercial enterprises organised as trusts. Both corporate unit trusts and public trading trusts are taxed as companies. Most public investment trusts are not corporate unit trusts or public trading trusts. The dividends reported excludes: - any dividends received by a partnership or trust, which is included at Question 10: Partnership and trusts (is_pt_net_dist_npp or is_pt_net_dist_pp). - any foreign source dividends, which is included at Question 16: Attributed foreign income. Dividend imputation From 1 July 1987, dividends paid to Australian shareholders by Australian companies, corporate unit trusts and public trading trusts have been taxed under the imputation system. Under this system, any dividends paid by resident companies that have paid Australian company taxes carry an imputation credit. These dividends are called franked dividends. The imputation credit is 39/61 times the franked amount of the dividend. If the taxpayer receives a franked dividend and is an Australian resident that are entitled to a rebate, this rebate will reduce the tax paid. However, the rebate cannot be refunded or used to reduce the Medicare levy. The Medicare levy will be calculated based on taxable income, which includes the amount of imputation credit. Non-resident individuals If the taxpayer is a non-resident, the franked dividends they receive are exempt from withholding tax and imputation credit cannot be refunded. Unfranked dividends are subject to withholding tax. They do not show their dividend income on the tax return. Expenses associated with earning dividends These are claimed under Question 27: Interested and dividend deductions (d_interest_div).
**Earliest Calculations**: For 1990-91, calculate the total franked amounts from each dividend.

column22:
Income from dividends: franked amount.

Dividends paid to shareholders by Australian resident companies are
taxed under a system known as ‘imputation’. It is called an imputation
system because the tax paid by a company may be imputed or attributed to
the shareholders. The tax paid by the company is allocated to
shareholders by way of franking credits attached to the dividends they
receive.

The basis of the system is that if a company pays or credits you with
dividends which have been franked, you may be entitled to a franking tax
offset for the tax the company has paid on its income. The franking tax
offset will cover or partly cover the tax payable on the dividends.

Dividends can be fully franked (meaning that the whole amount of the
dividend carries a franking credit) or partly franked (meaning that the
dividend has a franked amount and an unfranked amount). The dividend
statement or distribution statement you receive from the company paying
the franked dividend must state the amount of the franking credit and
the amounts of the franked and unfranked parts of the dividend.

Franked dividends have a franking/imputation credit attached to them.
column23:
For 1990-91, the variable refers to franked amounts on dividends where
the taxpayer was a shareholder in a company or held units in a corporate
unit trust or a public trading trust. A corporate unit trusts are public
trusts that are created as part of a reorganisation of a company. Public
trading trusts are commercial enterprises organised as trusts. Both
corporate unit trusts and public trading trusts are taxed as companies.
Most public investment trusts are not corporate unit trusts or public
trading trusts.

The dividends reported excludes:
- any dividends received by a partnership or trust, which is included at
Question 10: Partnership and trusts (is_pt_net_dist_npp or
is_pt_net_dist_pp).
- any foreign source dividends, which is included at Question 16:
Attributed foreign income.
Dividend imputation
From 1 July 1987, dividends paid to Australian shareholders by
Australian companies, corporate unit trusts and public trading trusts
have been taxed under the imputation system. Under this system, any
dividends paid by resident companies that have paid Australian company
taxes carry an imputation credit. These dividends are called franked
dividends. The imputation credit is 39/61 times the franked amount of
the dividend. If the taxpayer receives a franked dividend and is an
Australian resident that are entitled to a rebate, this rebate will
reduce the tax paid. However, the rebate cannot be refunded or used to
reduce the Medicare levy. The Medicare levy will be calculated based on
taxable income, which includes the amount of imputation credit.

Non-resident individuals
If the taxpayer is a non-resident, the franked dividends they receive
are exempt from withholding tax and imputation credit cannot be
refunded. Unfranked dividends are subject to withholding tax. They do
not show their dividend income on the tax return.

Expenses associated with earning dividends
These are claimed under Question 27: Interested and dividend deductions
(d_interest_div).

This variable refers to franked amounts on dividends and distributions
that were paid by Australian companies to taxpayers who owned shares.
These include:
- dividends applied under a dividend reinvestment plan
- dividends that were dealt with on your behalf
- bonus shares that qualify as dividends.

Dividends include distributions by a corporate limited partnership or
paid by a corporate unit trust, public trading trust, or listed
investment company. They can also include:
- earnings received, or were credited with, on a non-share equity
interest
- amounts received from, or were credited by, a private company as a
shareholder or an associate of a shareholder in the form of payments,
loans or debts forgiven (these are generally unfranked dividends)
- amounts received from, or were credited by, the trustee of a trust
estate in the form of payments, loans or debts forgiven where a private
company in which they were a shareholder, or an associate of a
shareholder, had an unpaid present entitlement (or was going to have
such an entitlement by a certain time) from the trust (these are
generally unfranked dividends).

The dividend amounts recorded under this variable is the dividends that
have a franking credit attached to them. Franking credits are amounts of
tax paid by the company that are allocated to the taxpayer’s dividend or
distributions. This franking credit can be claimed as a tax credit.
However, taxpayer might not be entitled to claim the franking credits
if:
- within 45 days of buying the shares (90 days for certain preference
shares), they either sold them or entered into an arrangement to reduce
the risk of making a loss on them (Holding period rule)
- they were under an obligation to make, or were likely to make, a
related payment (Related payments rule), or
- they received a dividend as a result of a dividend washing arrangement
(Dividend washing integrity rule).

If there are any shares in joint names, then only the proportion of
dividends is shown.   If the taxpayer:
- received a distribution from a partnership or trust, see Supplement
section question: Partnerships and trusts (is_pt_net_dist_pp or

- carried on a business of trading in shares and received income or

column22:
Amount of income earned by the taxpayer while being a full time student
less deductible expenses. Applicable if full-time education ceased for
the first time during the income year. Net income includes income earned
through salary and wages, non-salary and wage incomes, and income
received from their own business, partnerships, or beneficiary of a
trust.

If you left full-time education for the first time in a particular
financial year, you can only claim the tax-free threshold for the months
you were not studying full-time. However, if you were working while you
were studying, you can add on your net income for these months to work
out your tax-free threshold.

Note: The part-year tax free threshold for students that ceased fulltime
education in the income year was removed for the 2007 income year and
the label on the return form was discontinued.

and

- if full-time education stopped between 1 March 1991 and 30 June 1991,
and they did not begin another course of full-time education within four
months of stopping the earlier one.

### is_cg_net
**Form**: Individual Tax Return
**Section**: Supplementary section: Income
**Question**: Capital gain: Net Capital gain
**Label**: Net capital gains
**General Notes**: Net capital gain calculated as the taxpayers total capital gains less entitled discounts, concessions and current capital losses and unapplied net capital losses brought forward from prior income years. The “cost base” of an asset forms a fundamental step in determining whether a taxpayer has derived a capital gain or incurred a capital loss following the disposal of an asset. In its simplest form a taxable gain is calculated as the difference between the amount you receive upon disposal (“disposal consideration”) and the cost to you of the asset (“cost base”), indexed for inflation. Similarly a capital loss is calculated as the difference between the amount you paid (“cost base”) and the amount you receive upon disposal (“disposal consideration”). In determining the amount of a capital gain or capital loss, section 160Z of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (“the 1936 Act”) requires the taxpayer to compare the consideration received on the disposal of an asset with the asset’s cost base. Generally, a capital gain will arise where the disposal consideration exceeds the “cost base” (or “indexed cost base” where the asset was held for greater than 12 months). Alternatively, a capital loss will arise where the “reduced cost base” exceeds the disposal consideration.
**Latest or Current Conditions**: This variable refers to net capital gain made by the taxpayer. The taxpayer made a capital gain, or capital loss if a capital gains tax (CGT) event happened in the income year. A capital gain occurred if the amount of money and property received, or were entitled to receive, from the CGT event was more than the cost base of the asset and tax is paid on the capital gain. A capital loss occurred if the amount of money and property received, or were entitled to receive, from the CGT event was less than the reduced cost base of the asset. Examples of common CGT events are if the taxpayer sold or gave away a CGT asset, such as: - real estate, including family home, a holiday home, investment property, hobby farm or vacant block of land - shares - units in a unit trust or managed investment fund - forestry managed investment scheme interests (as a subsequent participant) - collectables, for example, jewellery - personal use assets. Other CGT events include: - an owned asset was lost or destroyed - an amount received for entering into an agreement, for example, you agreed not to work in a particular industry for a set period of time / - entering into a conservation covenant over land that they owned - receiving a non-assessable payment from a trust or company. Exceptions: This does not include any “listed investment company capital gain amount” included in a dividend paid by a listed investment company. This is reported under Question 8: Dividend deductions (d_div). If the taxpayer is a Norfolk Island resident, CGT may apply to assets acquired after 23 October 2015. The taxpayer cannot deduct a capital loss from their assessible income. Generally, a capital gain or loss is disregarded if it relates to: - assets acquired before 20 September 1985 - cars, motorcycles and similar vehicles - compensation received for personal injury - disposal of main residence - collectables, for example an antique or jewellery, which was acquired for $500 or less - the exchange of shares or units owned in a company or trust under a takeover, if certain conditions were met - shares in a company or interests in a trust where there had been a demerger and certain conditions had been met - disposal of an asset to which the small business 15-year exemption applies - disposal of certain investments by a venture capital limited partnership, an early stage venture capital limited partnership, or an Australian venture capital fund of funds - disposal of shares in a pooled development fund - personal use assets, such as boats, furniture, electrical goods and household items used or kept mainly for personal use or enjoyment. If it was acquired for more than $10,000, only capital losses is disregarded. If it was for $10,000 or less, then both capital gains and capital losses is disregarded. - transfer of an asset where the Small business restructure roll-over is available (gains or losses are deferred until the asset is disposed of).
**Latest or Current Calculations**: Step 1: Read the publication that is relevant to your circumstances and work out the amount of your capital gain or capital loss for each CGT event that occurred, and the amount of your capital gains from a trust (including a managed fund) for the income year. Step 2: Add up all your capital gains for the income year (except those that are disregarded) to work out your total current year capital gains. Do not apply yet capital losses, any CGT discounts or the small business concessions (other than the 15-year exemption). Write this amount at H item 18 (isn_cg_tot_current). Step 3: Work out your net capital gain or net capital loss. This is the amount remaining after applying to your current year capital gains whichever of the following items are relevant to you (in the order listed): / - capital losses in the income year / - unapplied net capital losses from earlier years / - any CGT discounts / - the small business 50% active asset reduction / - the small business retirement exemption or rollover. / / If the total amount remaining is positive or zero, write it at A item 18. If you have a negative amount, do not put anything at A. You have net capital losses to carry forward to later income years. Write the amount at V item 18 (isn_cg_loss_carry_fwd).
**Earliest Conditions**: For 1990-91, this variable refers to the net capital gain from assets sold or disposed of, or any other capital amounts received during the financial year. This also includes forfeited deposit or a capital gain distributed to a beneficiary of a trust. Net capital gain may be subject to capital gain tax. Capital gains tax may apply if the taxpayer sold or disposed of: - listed personal use assets, these includes assets owned for personal use and enjoyment and that cost more than $100 to buy. - non listed personal-use assets, these include any other assets that was owned for personal use and enjoyment and which was disposed of for more than $5000 each. - other assets, for example shares or units in unit trusts, options or rights to acquire shares or units, real estate (including holiday home), any other assets. Assets not subject to capital gains tax include: - most assets acquired before 20 September 1985. However, if any capital improvements were made to those assets after that date, capital gains may apply to those improvements. - in most cases, the taxpayer’s home - motor vehicles designed to carry less than nine passengers or one tonne - motorcycles. Taxpayer may offset current capital loss during the income year or for future income years.
**Earliest Calculations**: For 1990-91, For assets held less than 12 months: Capital gain = consideration received minus cost base. Capital loss = reduced cost base minus consideration received. For assets held more than 12 months: Capital gain = consideration received minus indexed cost base. Capital loss = reduced cost base minus consideration received. For non-listed personal-use assets: Similarly, but if the cost base or indexed cost base is less than $5000 it is taken to be $5000. Consideration received: amount received, or are entitled to receive for disposing of an asset or part of an asset. If the consideration is in form of property or gift, the consideration is the market value of the asset. Cost base: is the total of the cost of acquiring the assets, capital cost of maintaining a right over or title to the assets, costs of capital improvements (no repairs), and incidental costs (e.g. costs of advertising). Indexed cost base: applies if the asset was owned for more than 12 months. Multiply the cost base of the asset by it “indexing factor”. Reduced cost base: is the total of the cost base less allowable deductions plus relevant income (any amount that has been or will be included in assessable income as a result of the disposal of an asset and relating to income tax deductions that have been or are allowed in respect of the costs).

- the small business retirement exemption

small business 50% active asset reduction and the small business

of certain investments by a venture capital limited partnership, an
early stage venture capital limited partnership or an Australian venture

fund.

personal use assets, such as boats, furniture, electrical goods and
household items used or kept mainly for personal use or enjoyment. If

for $10,000 or less, both capital gains and capital losses is

This variable refers to net capital gain made by the taxpayer. The
taxpayer made a capital gain, or capital loss if a capital gains tax
(CGT) event happened in the income year. A capital gain occurred if the
amount of money and property received, or were entitled to receive, from
the CGT event was more than the cost base of the asset and tax is paid
on the capital gain. A capital loss occurred if the amount of money and
property received, or were entitled to receive, from the CGT event was
less than the reduced cost base of the asset.
Examples of common CGT events are if the taxpayer sold or gave away a
CGT asset, such as:
- real estate, including family home, a holiday home, investment
property, hobby farm or vacant block of land
- shares
- units in a unit trust or managed investment fund
- forestry managed investment scheme interests (as a subsequent
participant)
- collectables, for example, jewellery
- personal use assets.

Other CGT events include:
- an owned asset was lost or destroyed
- an amount received for entering into an agreement, for example, you
agreed not to work in a particular industry for a set period of time / -
entering into a conservation covenant over land that they owned
- receiving a non-assessable payment from a trust or company.

Exceptions:
This does not include any “listed investment company capital gain
amount” included in a dividend paid by a listed investment company. This
is reported under Question 8: Dividend deductions (d_div). If the
taxpayer is a Norfolk Island resident, CGT may apply to assets acquired
after 23 October 2015. The taxpayer cannot deduct a capital loss from
their assessible income.
Generally, a capital gain or loss is disregarded if it relates to:
- assets acquired before 20 September 1985
- cars, motorcycles and similar vehicles
- compensation received for personal injury
- disposal of main residence
- collectables, for example an antique or jewellery, which was acquired
for $500 or less
- the exchange of shares or units owned in a company or trust under a
takeover, if certain conditions were met
- shares in a company or interests in a trust where there had been a
demerger and certain conditions had been met
- disposal of an asset to which the small business 15-year exemption
applies
- disposal of certain investments by a venture capital limited
partnership, an early stage venture capital limited partnership, or an
Australian venture capital fund of funds
- disposal of shares in a pooled development fund
- personal use assets, such as boats, furniture, electrical goods and
household items used or kept mainly for personal use or enjoyment. If it
was acquired for more than $10,000, only capital losses is disregarded.
If it was for $10,000 or less, then both capital gains and capital
losses is disregarded.
- transfer of an asset where the Small business restructure roll-over is
available (gains or losses are deferred until the asset is disposed of).

work out the amount of your capital gain or capital loss for each CGT
event that occurred, and the amount of your capital gains from a trust
(including a managed fund) for the income year.
Step 2: Add up all your capital gains for the income year (except those
that are disregarded) to work out your total current year capital gains.
Do not apply yet capital losses, any CGT discounts or the small business
concessions (other than the 15-year exemption). Write this amount at H
item 18 (isn_cg_tot_current).
Step 3: Work out your net capital gain or net capital loss. This is the
amount remaining after applying to your current year capital gains
whichever of the following items are relevant to you (in the order
listed): / - capital losses in the income year / - unapplied net capital
losses from earlier years / - any CGT discounts / - the small business
50% active asset reduction / - the small business retirement exemption
or rollover. / / If the total amount remaining is positive or zero,
write it at A item 18. If you have a negative amount, do not put
anything at A. You have net capital losses to carry forward to later
income years. Write the amount at V item 18
(isn_cg_loss_carry_fwd).

**Form**: ATO

**Label**: ATO: div 293 tax - assessable income
**General Notes**: This is the amount of Division 293 income. Division 293 tax, started in income year 2013, is an additional tax on super contributions which reduces the tax concession for individuals whose combined income and contributions are greater than the Division 293 threshold. From 1 July 2017, the threshold at which a Division 293 tax calculation will result in an assessment being issued is $250,000. For 1 July 2012 to 30 June 2017, the threshold is $300,000. Division 293 tax is payable on the excess over the threshold, or on the Division 293 super contributions, whichever is less. The rate of Division 293 tax is 15%. The income component of the Division 293 tax calculation is based on the same income calculation used to determine if an individual needs to pay the Medicare levy surcharge (MLS), disregarding any reportable superannuation contributions reported on the tax return. The components of this income calculation are: - Taxable income (assessable income minus allowable deductions) - Total reportable fringe benefits amounts - Net financial investment loss - Net rental property loss - Net amount on which family trust distribution tax has been paid - Super lump sum taxed elements with a zero tax rate - Assessable first home super saver released amount. These amounts are added up (except the super lump sum and assessable first home super saver released amount, which are subtracted) to give the income amount.

### in_ess_foreign_disc
**Form**: Individual Tax Return
**Section**: Income
**Question**: Employee share schemes: Foreign source discounts
**Label**: Foreign source discounts on employee share schemes
**General Notes**: Foreign source discounts on employee share schemes. Refer to for more details.
**Latest or Current Conditions**: This variable refers to the foreign source discount on employee share scheme. The discount is the difference between the market value of the ESS interest and the amount paid to acquire them. If the taxpayer paid foreign income tax in respect to discounts received on ESS interest they may be entitled to claim a foreign income tax offset on the discount amounts where foreign income tax was paid. To claim the foreign income tax offset, they must also record an amount at item: Foreign income tax offset (see onra_foreign_tax) (for example, in tax return form 2017-18, see question 20). Examples of ESS interests are shares, stapled securities (provided at least one of the stapled interest is a share in a company, or the rights to acquire the shares or stapled securities. The ESS interests can be from an Australian or foreign company, related to employment inside or outside Australia, or related to a work relationship other than employment, for example sub-contracting. An ESS interest acquired by the taxpayer’s associate in respect to their employment is treated as though the ESS interest was acquired by the taxpayer. Changes to employee share schemes took effect on 1 July 2015 and apply to ESS interests acquired on or after that date. These changes include: - a tax concession through which some discounts on ESS interests in start-up companies will not be taxed under the employee share scheme regime, as long as the eligibility criteria are met. Subsequent gains on the disposal of these ESS interests will be taxed under the capital gain tax rules - changes to the ‘deferred taxing point’. Taxpayer may report ‘tax file number (TFN) amounts withheld’ if they did not provide their TFN or ABN to their employer. This is recorded under tw_ess. Excludes any ESS interests given by a start-up company. This amount is not shown on the Employee share scheme statement. If taxpayer qualifies as a temporary resident for tax, special rules may apply . If taxpayer disposed of any ESS interests due to a corporate restructure or takeover and received replacement shares, stapled securities or rights, provisions may apply.
**Latest or Current Calculations**: Add up all foreign discount amounts from employee share scheme interest.
**Earliest Conditions**: For 2009-10, this variable refers to the foreign source discount on employee share scheme. The discount is the difference between the market value of the ESS interest and the amount paid to acquire them. If the taxpayer paid foreign income tax in respect to discounts received on ESS interest they may be entitled to claim a foreign income tax offset on the discount amounts where foreign income tax was paid. To claim the foreign income tax offset, they must also record an amount at item 20: Foreign income tax offset (see onra_foreign_tax). Examples of ESS interests are shares, stapled securities (provided at least one of the stapled interest is a share in a company, or the rights to acquire the shares or stapled securities. ### i_ess
**Form**: Individual Tax Return

**Question**: Employee Share Schemes: Total assessable discount amount
**Label**: Total assessable discount amount from Employee Share Schemes
**General Notes**: Total assessable income from taxed upfront and deferred tax Employee Share Schemes less any applicable deductions. Employee Share Schemes (ESS) give employees: - shares in the company they work for at a discounted price - the opportunity to buy shares in the company in the future (this is called a right or option). The discount you received on the market value for ESS interests needs to be included in your tax return as assessable income.
**Latest or Current Conditions**: This variable refers to the total assessable discount amount on Employee Share Schemes, which is made up from discounts on ‘Employee Share Scheme interests’ (ESS interest) that the taxpayer received under a Employee Share Scheme net any reductions. This may include Discount from tax upfront schemes - ineligible for reduction (see in_ess_disc_inelgbl) and/or Discount from tax upfront schemes - eligible for reduction (see in_ess_disc_elgbl), Discount from deferral schemes (see in_ess_disc_defer), and Discount on ESS interest acquired pre 1 July 2009 and ‘cessation time’ occurred during financial year (see in_ess_interest_pre_2009). Examples of ESS interests are shares, stapled securities (provided at least one of the stapled interest is a share in a company, or the rights to acquire the shares or stapled securities. The ESS interests can be from an Australian or foreign company, related to employment inside or outside Australia, or related to a work relationship other than employment, for example sub-contracting. An ESS interest acquired by the taxpayer’s associate in respect to their employment is treated as though the ESS interest was acquired by the taxpayer. The discount is the difference between the market value of the ESS interest and the amount paid to acquire them. The taxpayer will be taxed on the discount in the year in which the interest was acquired. Such schemes are known as ‘taxed-upfront schemes’. However, if certain conditions relating to the taxpayer and their scheme is met, the taxing point is deferred until a later time. These tax-deferred schemes are known as ‘deferral schemes’. Changes to Employee Share Schemes took effect on 1 July 2015 and apply to ESS interests acquired on or after that date. These changes include: - a tax concession through which some discounts on ESS interests in start-up companies will not be taxed under the Employee Share Scheme regime, as long as the eligibility criteria are met. Subsequent gains on the disposal of these ESS interests will be taxed under the capital gain tax rules - changes to the ‘deferred taxing point’. Taxpayer may report ‘tax file number (TFN) amounts withheld’ if they did not provide their TFN or ABN to their employer. This is recorded under tw_ess. Excludes any ESS interests given by a start-up company. This amount is not shown on the Employee share scheme statement. If taxpayer qualifies as a temporary resident for tax, special rules may apply if they acquired ESS interests under pre-1 July 2009 Employee Share Scheme rules or ESS interests under an Employee Share Scheme If taxpayer disposed of any ESS interests due to a corporate restructure or takeover and received replacement shares, stapled securities or rights, provisions may apply.
**Latest or Current Calculations**: Option 1: if taxpayer does not have any Discount from tax upfront schemes - eligible for reduction (see in_ess_disc_elgbl), the total assessable amount is the sum of Discount from tax upfront schemes - ineligible for reduction (see in_ess_disc_inelgbl), Discount from deferral schemes (see in_ess_disc_defer), and Discount on ESS interest acquired pre 1 July 2009 and ‘cessation time’ occurred during financial year (see in_ess_interest_pre_2009). Option 2: if taxpayer reports any Discount from tax upfront schemes - eligible for reduction (see in_ess_disc_elgbl), they may be entitled to a reduction of up to $1,000 on the amount they are assessed on. (ds_pers_super_cont).

satisfy the income test and are not entitled to a reduction. Therefore,

**Form**: Individual Tax Return

**Question**: Government super contributions: Other deductions from business income
**Label**: Other deductions from business income for government super contributions adjustments
**General Notes**: Other business deductions for taxpayers who are eligible for super co-contribution (which was introduced in July 2003) or low income super contribution (which was introduced in July 2012) or low income super tax offset (which was introduced in July 2017). Includes business deductions other than those reported in Business and Professional Items from P8 (Business income and expenses). Examples include partnership loss calculated in labour hire payments, personal services income deductions or other deductions against business income.
**Latest or Current Conditions**: This variable refers to other business deductions for taxpayers who are eligible for super co-contribution, low income super contribution, or low income super tax offset. To claim, taxpayer must be eligible for: Super co-contribution, i.e. , for example for 2017-18, if taxpayer has - made an eligible personal super contribution (for which you are not claiming a deduction) - did not exceed your non-concessional contribution cap - total superannuation balance at 30 June 2017 was less than $1,600,000 - under 71 years old on 30 June 2018 - taxable income less than $51,813, and - at least some income from employment or business (including partnership) - did not hold a temporary visa at any time during 2017-18 (unless it is a New Zealand citizenship or it was a prescribed visa). Or low income super contribution or low income super tax offset, i.e., for example for 2017-18, if taxpayer has: - adjusted taxable income (ATI) less than or equal to $37,000 - concessional contributions made to complying super fund, and - 10% or more of total income from employment and/or business income (including partnership). And received income from a partnership shown at Partnership and Trusts in supplementary tax return form. Furthermore, taxpayer has - had business deductions in the income year other than those included in the deductions items at item P8 in the Business and professional items schedule. Examples include: share of partnership loss, deductions relating to partnership distribution, personal service income deductions, or deductions related to managing your business tax affairs.
**Latest or Current Calculations**: Total amount of business deductions other than those reported in Business and Professional Items from P8.

**Form**: Individual Tax Return
**Section**: Income
**Question**: Eligible termination payment: excessive component
**Label**: Excessive component of eligible termination payment
**General Notes**: Excessive component of eligible termination payment.
**Latest or Current Conditions**: Latest year: 2006-07. This variable refers to an eligible termination payment (ETP), which includes: - a lump sum payment from your employer when the taxpayer retired or ceased employment - a lump sum payment from a superannuation fund, approved deposit fund, retirement savings account or life insurance company - a similar payment to those above, paid as the beneficiary of a person who has died. This is called a ‘death benefit ETP’. However, if the payments were made to the taxpayer as the trustee of a deceased estate they must be shown on the trust tax return, not on your personal tax return - a payment from the Tax Office of amounts collected from an employer either by way of Superannuation Guarantee Charge payments or payments to the Superannuation Holding Accounts Special Account. Lump sum payment from employer includes: - a payment in lieu of notice or a golden handshake - a payment for unused sick leave or unused rostered days off - compensation for loss of a job or wrongful dismissal - a redundancy payment or an approved early retirement scheme payment that exceeded the tax free threshold - a payment received because of invalidity - a similar payment paid to the trustee of a deceased estate after the death of an employee. An ETP also includes a payments from a superannuation fund, an approved deposit fund or a life insurance company such as: - payments, other than a pension or annuity, from a superannuation fund - payments received when a pension or annuity is changed into a lump sum - payments made to the trustee of a deceased estate. Lump sum payment received on termination of foreign employment and from a non-resident superannuation fund is recorded at item 19: Foreign source income and foreign assets or property (see isn_fsi_assessable_inc). The taxpayer may have the option to roll-over their ETP. This means transferring all or part of their ETP to a complying superannuation fund or an approved deposit fund or buying an annuity. This is not recorded under i_etp. A reasonable benefit limit (RBL) is the maximum amount of superannuation benefit that is taxed at concessional (or reduced) rates. Anything above the RBL is taxed at the marginal tax rate and is called the excessive amount.

**Label**: Deductible amount of undeducted purchase price (UPP) of an Australian pension or annuity
**General Notes**: Deduction claim amount for pension or annuity contributions for which a deduction has not previously been claimed. The undeducted purchase price (UPP) is the amount contributed towards the purchase price of the pension or annuity for which a tax deduction could not or has not been claimed. The deductible amount, calculated using UPP, can be used to reduce yearly taxable income from pension or annuity.
**Latest or Current Conditions**: Latest year: 2006-07. If taxpayers showed income from an Australian pension or annuity at item 7: ‘Other Australian pensions or annuities - including superannuation pensions’ (i_annuities) on tax return, they may be able to reduce the amount of taxable income that they have to pay tax on if the Australian pension or annuity has a UPP. did you own, or have an interest in assets located outside Australia,
which had a total value of AUD$50,000 or more?
column21:
Indicator of interest in assets located outside Australia with total
value of AUD$50,000 or more
column22:
Binary indicator of whether the taxpayer held any interest in assets
located outside Australia with total value of AUD$50,000 or more.
column23:
For 1999-2000, this variable is a binary indicator of whether the
taxpayer had interest in assets located outside Australia with total
value of AUD$50,000 or more during the income year. Assets include real
estate, shares in companies and other entities, interests in
partnerships or trusts, businesses, debentures, bonds, money and funds
held in accounts or by other parties, loans to other parties and
deposits. They also include intangible property such as trademarks,
copyrights, patents, debtors or ‘equitable choses in action’. Assets
also include any interest, whether legal or beneficial, and whether held
directly or indirectly through one or more interposed entities.
column25:
For 1999-2000, print X in the Yes box if the value of overseas assets
was AUD$50,000 or more. Otherwise print X in the No box.
column30:
**2000**: Major; Introduced; New variable.

**2001**: Moderate; Component; Excludes assets held overseas covered by
question 18 Foreign entities (is_cfc).

column31:
This variable is a binary indicator of whether the taxpayer had interest
in assets located outside Australia with total value of AUD$50,000 or
more during the income year. Assets include real estate, shares in
companies and other entities, interests in partnerships or trusts,
businesses, debentures, bonds, money and funds held in accounts or by
other parties, loans to other parties and deposits. They also include
intangible property such as trademarks, copyrights, patents, debtors or
‘equitable choses in action’. Assets also include any interest, whether
legal or beneficial, and whether held directly or indirectly through one
or more interposed entities. This excludes any assets held overseas
covered under question 19 Foreign entities (is_cfc).
column32:
Print X in the Yes box if the value of overseas assets was AUD$50,000 or
more. Otherwise print X in the No box.

### is_bus_pp
**Form**: Individual Tax Return
**Section**: Supplementary section: Income
**Question**: Net income or loss from business: Primary production
**Label**: Net income or loss from primary production business
**General Notes**: Net primary production income or loss amount from business activities. Reported by taxpayers that are required to complete the business and professional items schedule. For income tax purposes " Primary Production " refers to a business of " Farming “, and hence the term” Primary Producer “;” Non-Primary Production " refers to a business that is not related to " Farming ". Primary production business activities include: - cultivating or propagating plants, fungi or their products or parts (including seeds, spores, bulbs and similar things) in any physical environment. - manufacturing dairy produce from raw material that \[the taxpayer\] produced; - felling trees in a planation or forest and planting or tending trees in a plantation or forest that are intended to be felled. - maintaining animals for the purpose of selling them or their bodily produce, including natural increase. The relevant indicators used by the ATO in determining whether an activity is a business of primary production are outlined in Taxation Ruling TR 97/11 - Income Tax: am I carrying on a business of primary production?
**Latest or Current Conditions**: This variable refers to income or loss derived from primary production activities. Primary production specific income includes income from: - cultivating or propagating plants, fungi or their products or parts (including seeds, spores, bulbs and similar things) in any physical environment - maintaining animals for the purpose of selling them or their bodily produce, including natural increase - manufacturing dairy produce from raw material - fishing or pearling - tree farming or felling.
**Latest or Current Calculations**: The net income/loss from primary production is recorded under item P8: Business income and expenses on page 11 as total business income net total expenses taking into account reconciliation items and deferred non-comercial business losses from previous year. Total business income includes: P8-D: Gross payments where Australian business number not quoted; P8-B: Gross payments subject to foreign resident withholding (excluding capital gains); P8-F: Gross payments - voluntary agreement; P8-O: Gross payments - labour; P8-H: assessable government industry payments; P8-J: Other business expenses. Total business expenses includes: Opening cost of sales, foreign resident withholding expenses (excluding capital gains), contractor, subcontractor and commission expenses, superannuation expenses, bad debts, lease expenses, rent expenses, interest expenses within Australian, interest expenses overseas, depreciation expenses, motor vehicle expenses, repairs and maintenance, and all other expenses. Reconciliation items include: Section 40-880 deduction, business deduction for project pool, landcare operations and business deduction for decline in value of water facility, fencing asset and fodder storage asset, income reconciliation adjustment, expense reconciliation adjustments.
**Earliest Conditions**: For 1990-91, this variable refers to any income or loss from primary production activities. Primary production includes production from cultivating the land, keeping and breeding animals or poultry to sell them or their produce, fishing operation, forest operations, and manufacture of dairy produce by the dairy farmer.
**Earliest Calculations**: For 1990-91, the net income/loss from primary production activities is calculated as the gross primary production business income minus total primary business deductions. Gross primary production is transferred from the ‘Income Tax and primary producers’ notes and worksheet’. Total primary production deductions include salary and wages paid, payment to contractors, depreciation of assets, interest paid on money borrowed for business use, motor vehicle expenses, repairs, lease payments and other business related expenses related to primary production.
**URL Address**: NA
**Type**: Numerical
**Form Location**: 1991(Pg2_11F),1992(Pg2_12B),1993(Pg2_11B),1994(Pg2_11B),1995(Pg2_11B),1996(Pg2_11B),1997(Pg3_11B),1998(Pg8_11B),1999(Pg6_11B),2000(Pg8_12B),2001(Pg6_11B),2002(Pg6_11B),2003(Pg6_11B),2004(Pg6_11B),2005(Pg6_14B),2006(Pg6_14B),2007(Pg6_14B),2008(Pg6_15B),2009(Pg6_15B),2010(Pg7_15B),2011(Pg7_15B),2012(Pg8_15B),2013(pg9_15B),2014(pg9_15B),2015(pg9_15B),2016(pg9_15B),2017(Pg9_15B),2018(Pg9_15B),2019(Pg9_15B),2020(Pg9_15B),2021(Pg9_15B),2022(Pg9_15B)
**Event time line: Significance, Type of change(s), Description of change(s)**: **1992**: Minor; Component; Total primary production business income includes total business income from primary production during the income year. This also includes profit made on disposal of depreciable assets, sales of trading stock, service income and fees, delivery charges and commission revenue related to primary production business. This excludes: - Dividend income, reported at Question 19 Dividends (i_div_frank and i_div_unfrank) - Income from rent, reported at Question 18 Rent, premiums, etc (isn_gross_rent) - Income from capital gains, reported at Question 15 Net capital gain (is_cg_net) - Royalties - Interest income, reported at Question 10 Interest (i_interest) - Attributed foreign income, reported at Question 16 Attributed foreign income (is_cfc). - Foreign source income, reported at Question 17 General net foreign source income (is_fsi_other_foreign_incl_rent). - Foreign exchange profit/loss - Income from a partnership or trust, reported at Question 11 Partnership and trusts (is_pt_net_dist_npp). Calculation Business income and deductions for primary and non-primary production are now recorded in the Business/professional declaration items Item 44 Business income and deductions on page 4. Expense categories are recorded separately and include: External labour costs (44E), cost of sales (44F), total interest expenses (44G), depreciation expenses (44H), motor vehicle expenses (44I), repairs and maintenances (44J), land degradation expenses (44K) and all other expenses (44L). Employers are also entitled to a deduction for contributions made to a superannuation, provident, benefit, or retirement fund for the benefit of eligible employees or their dependents. This is reported under all other expenses (44L). Net income/loss from primary production business is calculated as total business income less expenses add reconciliation adjustments (44N). Reconciliation adjustments reconciles the business operating profit or loss with the business taxable income. **1993**: Minor; Component; Expenses categories added include: Superannuation category (48G) and separate categories for lease (48J) and rent expenses (48K) added under Item 48 Business income and deductions on page 4. **1994**: Minor; Component; Investment allowances is added to net income/loss from business under item 47 Business income and deductions (47R). Investment allowances is calculated as 10% of the capital cost of acquiring or constructing new items of plant which costs $3,000 or more and quality for the general investment allowance. This is added to net income/loss from business. **1995**: Minor; Component; Also includes those who received income under the reportable payment system. Any taxable income earned as an artist, composer, inventor, performer, production associate, active sportsperson or writer must also include their eligible taxable income at Question 19 Other income - eligible taxable income (see isn_prof_taxable_inc). This amount will only be taxed once. **1996**: Minor; Component; Investment allowance discontinued from item 54 Business income and deductions. **1997**: Minor; Component; Contractor, sub-contractor and commission expenses added to item 54 Business Income and deductions on page 6. Investment allowances added back in to item 54 Business income and deductions. **1998**: Moderate; Component; An activity is generally defined to be business in nature if it: - has actually commenced - has a significant commercial purpose or character - is undertaken in a business-like manner - results in a profit - is carried out in a manner that is characteristic of the industry - has repetition, regularity or continuity - cannot be more properly described as a hobby. Total business income from primary production is the sum gross RPS income (P6F), assessable government industry payments (P6H), and other business income (P6J) recorded under Item P6 Business income and expenses under 1998 Business and professional items schedule. Gross reportable payment system (RPS) income is the total amount of RPS income derived from primary and non-primary production. RPS applies to certain payments made in the fishing, clothing, smash repair, and from 1 March 1997, fruit and vegetable industries. Any assessable government industry payments, include any payments that are assessable income received from government sources that has been paid as a result of non-primary business activities such as bounties, diesel fuel rebate, drought relief, employee subsidies, export incentive grants, Medicare payments to medical practices. Other business income includes gross sales of trading stock, goods taken for own use from stock, gross earnings from services, bad debt recovered, profit on sale of depreciable assets, royalties, insurance recoveries, subsidies, employee contributions for fringe benefits, and non-assessable government assistance from all sources. Expenses Interest expenses split into interest expenses within Australia (P6Q) and interest expenses earned overseas (P6R) under Item P6 Business income and expenses under 1998 Business and professional items schedule. Reconciliation items include drought investment allowances (P6U) calculated as 10% of the cost of new property to fight the effects of drought (limit of $5,000), environment protection or environmental impact study expenses (P6V), landcare operations and water conservation/conveying expenses (P6W) and other reconciliation adjustments (P6X). **2000**: Minor; Component; Reconciliation item ‘other reconciliation adjustments’ split into income reconciliation adjustments (P6X) and expense reconciliation adjustment (P6H). Income reconciliation adjustments includes income add backs - income not shown in the profit or loss statement but is assessable and income subtractions - income shown in the profit or loss statement but is not assessable income. Expense reconciliation adjustments include expense add backs - expenses shown in the accounts which are not tax deductible and expense subtractions - items shown as expenses which are deductible for expense purposes. **2001**: Major; Component; New categorisation of primary production income reported under item P8 business income and expenses on page 10. New categories include: - income under a Pay As You Go (PAYG) voluntary agreement (P8F) - income from which an amount was withheld because they did not quote their Australian Business Number (ABN) (P8D) - income as an independent contractor under a labour hire arrangement or income from a specified payment including payment for tutorial services provided for the Aboriginal Tutorial Assistance Scheme of the Department of Education, Training and Youth Affairs, and payment for translation and interpretation services for the Translating and Interpreting Service of the Department of Immigration and Multicultural Affairs (P8O) If they are self-employed, or driving a taxi under a standard bailment agreement with an owner/operator. Excludes any income reported under Question 13 Net personal services income (is_psi_net). Primary production business includes: - cultivating or propagating plants, fungi or their products or parts - maintaining animals for the purpose of selling them or their bodily produce - manufacturing dairy produce from raw material you produced - conducting operations relating directly to taking or catching fish, turtles, dugong, bêche-de-mer, crustaceans or aquatic molluscs - conducting operations relating directly to taking or culturing pearls or pearl shell - planting or tending trees in a plantation or forest that are intended to be felled - felling trees in a plantation or forest - transporting trees felled in a plantation or forest to the place where they are first to be milled or processed or from which they are to be transported to the place where they are first to be milled or processed. **2002**: Minor; Component; Section 80-880 deduction (P8A) and business deduction for project pool (P8L) added to reconciliation items and Environmental impact assessment and environmental protection expenses changed to Deduction for environmental protection expenses at item P8 Business income and expenses on page 10. **2003**: Minor; Component; Income from a specified payment includes income as a performing artist in a promotional activity. Other business income includes those received as a sole trader. Drought investment allowance removed from reconciliation items in item P8 Business income and expenses. **2005**: Minor; Component; Gross payments subject to foreign resident withholding (P8B) is added to income and foreign withholding expenses (P8U) is added to expenses under P8 Business income and expenses on page 10. If the taxpayer was 55 years or older on 30 June 2005, they may be entitled to the mature age worker tax offset. Any business income or loss will need to be reported at M Question T12 Net income from working **2006**: Minor; Component; If the taxpayer derived income from business under the simplified tax system (STS), they may be eligible to claim the entrepreneurs tax offset. Net STS income is reported under N item T14 Entrepreneurs tax offset - net simplified tax system income. **2008**: Minor; Component; If the taxpayer derived income from a business and quality for the small business entity concession, they may be eligible to claim the entrepreneurs tax offset. Generally a sole trader, partnership or trust is a small business entity for the 2007-08 income year if its aggregated turnover was less than $2 million. **2009**: Minor; Component; Small business and general business tax break in the form of an investment allowance is (P8F) added to Reconciliation items at item P8 Business income and expenses on page 10. **2013**: Minor; Component; Deduction for environmental protection expenses, small business and general business tax break removed from Reconciliation items under item P8 Business income and expenses on page 12. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

sales of trading stock, service income and fees, delivery charges and

Calculation Business income and deductions for primary and non-primary
production are now recorded in the Business/professional declaration
items Item 44 Business income and deductions on page 4.

Expense categories are recorded separately and include: External labour
costs (44E), cost of sales (44F), total interest expenses (44G),
depreciation expenses (44H), motor vehicle expenses (44I), repairs and
maintenances (44J), land degradation expenses (44K) and all other
expenses (44L). Employers are also entitled to a deduction for
contributions made to a superannuation, provident, benefit, or
retirement fund for the benefit of eligible employees or their
dependents. This is reported under all other expenses (44L).

Net income/loss from primary production business is calculated as total
business income less expenses add reconciliation adjustments (44N).

deductions on page 4.

under the reportable payment system.

their eligible taxable income at Question 19 Other income - eligible
taxable income (see isn_prof_taxable_inc). This amount will only be
taxed once.

expenses added to item 54 Business Income and deductions on page 6.

deductions.

**1998**: Moderate; Component; An activity is generally defined to be
business in nature if it:
- has actually commenced
- has a significant commercial purpose or character
- is undertaken in a business-like manner
- results in a profit
- is carried out in a manner that is characteristic of the industry
- has repetition, regularity or continuity
- cannot be more properly described as a hobby.
Total business income from primary production is the sum gross RPS
income (P6F), assessable government industry payments (P6H), and other
business income (P6J) recorded under Item P6 Business income and
expenses under 1998 Business and professional items schedule.

Gross reportable payment system (RPS) income is the total amount of RPS
income derived from primary and non-primary production. RPS applies to
certain payments made in the fishing, clothing, smash repair, and from 1
March 1997, fruit and vegetable industries.

Any assessable government industry payments, include any payments that
are assessable income received from government sources that has been
paid as a result of non-primary business activities such as bounties,
diesel fuel rebate, drought relief, employee subsidies, export incentive
grants, Medicare payments to medical practices.

Other business income includes gross sales of trading stock, goods taken
for own use from stock, gross earnings from services, bad debt
recovered, profit on sale of depreciable assets, royalties, insurance
recoveries, subsidies, employee contributions for fringe benefits, and
non-assessable government assistance from all sources.

Expenses Interest expenses split into interest expenses within Australia

income and expenses under 1998 Business and professional items schedule.

calculated as 10% of the cost of new property to fight the effects of
drought (limit of $5,000), environment protection or environmental
impact study expenses (P6V), landcare operations and water
conservation/conveying expenses (P6W) and other reconciliation
adjustments (P6X).

subtractions - items shown as expenses which are deductible for expense

- income as an independent contractor under a labour hire arrangement or

Primary production business includes:

produce

- conducting operations relating directly to taking or catching fish,
turtles, dugong, bêche-de-mer, crustaceans or aquatic molluscs
- conducting operations relating directly to taking or culturing pearls
or pearl shell
- planting or tending trees in a plantation or forest that are intended
to be felled
- felling trees in a plantation or forest
- transporting trees felled in a plantation or forest to the place where
they are first to be milled or processed or from which they are to be
transported to the place where they are first to be milled or
processed.

changed to Deduction for environmental protection expenses at item P8
Business income and expenses on page 10.

Drought investment allowance removed from reconciliation items in item
P8 Business income and expenses.

**2005**: Minor; Component; Gross payments subject to foreign resident

**Label**: Retirement phase events: balance transfers to reversionary income stream
**General Notes**: Retirement phase events: balance transfers to reversionary income stream, recorded in the transfer balance account. Reversionary income stream is a superannuation income stream that automatically reverts to a nominated beneficiary on the death of its current recipient. The date of death of the original member is when the income stream first becomes payable to the beneficiary. The transfer balance account records your retirement phase interests and you will only have one transfer balance account for all your retirement phase interests. It will remain active until your death. The transfer balance account is a record of the events that count towards your personal transfer balance cap (earnings are exempt from tax). Your transfer balance account commences on either: - the day you first receive a retirement phase income stream, after 1 July 2017 - 1 July 2017, if you were already receiving a retirement phase income stream on 30 June 2017. The transfer balance cap applies from 1 July 2017. It is a lifetime limit on the total amount of capital that individuals can transfer into the retirement phase that are exempt from tax to support their super income streams. In 2017–18, the general transfer balance cap was $1.6 million. It is subject to indexation in $100,000 increments on an annual basis in line with the consumer price index (CPI), rounded down to the nearest $100,000. Your increment in personal balance cap is based on the indexation on the unsued personal cap. If at any stage you have used all your cap, then indexation will not apply to you. Your increment in personal balance cap is based on the indexation on the unsued personal cap. If at any stage you have used all your cap, then indexation will not apply to you. **Label**: Education tax refund - refundable tax offset claimed.
**General Notes**: Education tax refund offset amount the taxpayer is eligible to claim for education expenses for the primary and secondary school studies of a child or for education expenses of the taxpayer if the taxpayer is an independent student under 25 years old.
**Latest or Current Conditions**: Latest year: 2010-11. This variable refers to the education tax refund (ETR) offset amount the taxpayer is eligible to claim for education expenses for the primary or secondary school studies of a child or for education expenses of the taxpayer if the taxpayer is an independent student under 25 years old. To be eligible to claim the ETR, the taxpayer must have met one of the four conditions and the student must have met the school requirement. Condition 1: Taxpayer or partner received or eligible to receive Family Tax Benefit (FTB) Part A for their child. Condition 2: Taxpayer or partner received payments other than FTB for that child. This includes a social security pension or benefit, a Labour Market Program payment, or a prescribed educational scheme payment. Condition 3: The child was 16 years or older, was not attending primary or secondary school studies and did not earn any income during the income year. Condition 4: Taxpayer is an independent student if they were under 25 years old and were receiving a social security pension or benefit, a Labour Market Program payment or a prescribed educational scheme payment, they met the independence requirements for the payment, they were an Australian resident (under the Social Security Act 1991) or a special category visa holder (under the Migration Act 1958), were residing in Australia, and no one else, such as a parent or an approved care organisation, was entitled to the ETR on their behalf. (See TaxPack 2011 for more details).

**Latest or Current Conditions**: This variable refers to deferred non-commercial business losses if during the income year, the taxpayer conducted a business activity as a partner in a partnership which resulted in a loss or resulted in a loss after deducting expenses. There are special rules relating to the deferral of non-commercial business losses. This applies to both Australian and foreign business activities. Any loss during the income year from business activities as a sole trader or partnership can be used to calculate the current taxable income if: - an exceptions applies - taxpayer meets the income requirement and one of the four tests is satisfied, or - the Commissioner has exercised his discretion or ruled that it will be exercised to allow a claim on loss. ### isn_fmd_deposits
**Form**: Individual Tax Return
**Section**: Supplementary section: Income
**Question**: Net farm management deposits or repayments: Deductible deposits
**Label**: Total deductible farm management deposits
**General Notes**: Total amount of deductible deposits made by the taxpayer in the respective income year.
**Latest or Current Conditions**: This variable refers to the total farm management deductible deposits made during the income year. This amount is used to calculate farm management deposit tax concession. The taxpayer may be eligible for the farm management deposit (FMD) tax concession if they received a distribution of income as a beneficiary of a trust that carried on a business of primary production. Farm management deposits are deductible if, during the income year, the taxpayer (FMD owner) satisfied the following: - taxable non-primary production income is under a threshold amount (for example, in 2017-18: it is $100,000 or less) - was carrying on a primary production business at the time of making the deposit - if they stopped carrying on a primary production business during the year, they recommenced carrying on such a business within 120 days - individual deposits were not less than a given individual limit and total deposit was not more than a given account limit (for example, in 2017-18: individual limit is $1,000 and account limit is $800,000) - individual deposits did not cause your total FMDs to exceed the account limit - individual deposits did not exceed the amount of taxable primary production income in that year - they held the deposits for at least 12 months or qualify for the early repayment exceptions. Some deposits cannot be deducted if they were made in the year and during the year the FMD owner: - became bankrupt or ceased to carry on a primary production business (including a business that was carried on by a partnership or by a trust) for 120 days or more, or - died. Deposits that were paid within 12 months are also non-deductible.
**Latest or Current Calculations**: Add up deductible deposits made during the income year.
**Earliest Conditions**: For 2011-12, this variable refers to the total farm management deductive deposits made during the income year. This amount is used to calculate farm management deposit tax concession. The taxpayer may be eligible for the farm management deposit (FMD) tax concession if they received a distribution of income as a beneficiary of a trust that carried on a business of primary production. Farm management deposits are deductible if, during the income year, the taxpayer (FMD owner)satisfied the following: - taxable non-primary production income is $65,000 or less - was carrying on a primary production business at the time of making the deposit - if they stopped carrying on a primary production business during the year, they recommenced carrying on such a business within 120 days - individual deposits were not less than $1,000 and total deposits not more than $400,000 - individual deposits did not cause your total FMDs to exceed the $400,000 account limit - individual deposits did not exceed the amount of taxable primary production income in that year - they held the deposits for at least 12 months or qualify for the early repayment exceptions. Some deposits cannot be deducted if they were made in the year and during the year the FMD owner: - became bankrupt or ceased to carry on a primary production business (including a business that was carried on by a partnership or by a trust) for 120 days or more, or - died. Deposits that were paid within 12 months are also non-deductible.
**Earliest Calculations**: For 2011-12, add up deductible deposits made during the income year.

### i_annuities
**Form**: Individual Tax Return
**Section**: Income
**Question**: Other Australian pensions or annuities: including superannuation pension
**Label**: Gross payments of other Australian pensions or annuities - including superannuation pension
**General Notes**: Gross payments of other Australian pensions or annuities - including superannuation pension. Reporting of superannuation income stream benefits significantly changed from the 2008 income year, with taxpayers required to report both the taxed element and untaxed elements of the taxable income component of the income stream benefit. From the 2008 income year onwards, the values previously captured in the variable i_annuities were separated into new variables i_annuities_txd and i_annuities_untxd as the taxed and untaxed elements were separately identified for the first time. Note: The superannuation income stream benefits amount classified as the tax-free component is non-assessable non-exempt income and not included in the calculation of taxable income.
**Latest or Current Conditions**: Latest year: 2006-07. This variable refers to income from Australian annuity, superannuation, or other pensions and therefore may be eligible to receive a rebate on taxed payments. Australian annuity, superannuation, or other pensions include: - superannuation and similar pensions and annuities paid by an Australian superannuation fund, life issurance company or retirement savings account (RSA) provider, and - pensions paid by a fund established for the benefit of Commonwealth, state or territory employees and their dependents - for example funds managed by ComSuper or VIcSuper. Does not include pensions recorded under question 6: Australian Government pensions and allowances (i_gov_pension). Deductions and tax offsets eligible on annuity payments include: - deduction on the undeducted purchase price of an Australian annuity recorded under d_aust_pension_upp - senior Australian tax offset, see on_sato_cd - tax offset on superannuation annuity or pensions recorded under onra_super_inc_stream.

The rebate may be claimed on taxable annuities or pensions and must have started payments from or after 1 July 1988.
