### is_fsi_pension_upp
**Form**: Individual Tax Return
**Section**: Supplementary section: Income
**Question**: Foreign source income and foreign assets or property: Net foreign pensions or annuity income WITH an undeducted purchase price
**Label**: Net foreign pension or annuity income with an undeducted purchase price
**General Notes**: Taxable foreign pension or annuity income with an undeducted purchase price less deductible expenses incured in gaining foreign pensions and annuities, excluding any interest or borrowing costs. Whereby, incurred is defined as: 1) received a bill or invoice for an expense that you are liable for and must pay (even if you don’t pay it until after the end of the income year) or 2) do not receive a bill or invoice but you are charged and you pay for the expense. Note: You can claim a deduction to reduce the taxable amount on income you receive from a foreign pension or annuity that has an undeducted purchase price (UPP). Only some foreign pensions and annuities have a UPP. The UPP is the amount you contribute towards the purchase price of your pension or annuity – your personal contributions. The part of your annual pension or annuity income which represents a return to you of your personal contributions is tax-free. This tax-free portion is the deductible amount of the UPP. If you receive a foreign pension or annuity and you want to know the amount you can claim a deduction for in relation to the UPP, you need to fill form: “Request for a determination of the deductible amount of UPP of a foreign pension or annuity”.\\
**Latest or Current Conditions**: This variable refers to income from taxable foreign pension or annuity with an undeducted purchase price. Most foreign pensions and annuities are taxable in Australia, even if tax was withheld from your payment by the country from which the payment came. Taxpayer may claim a foreign income tax offset at this item if: - the country from which their foreign pension or annuity came withheld tax from payment; - they were not entitled to seek a refund of the foreign tax from that country and; - the foreign pension or annuity is also taxable in Australia.
**Latest or Current Calculations**: Step 1 If you are not going to claim a refund of foreign tax paid from the country which paid your foreign pension or annuity, you need to add the amount of foreign tax to the amount of foreign pension or annuity you received. Step 2 Sort your foreign pensions and annuities into those with an undeducted purchase price (UPP) and those without a UPP. Step 3 Add up all foreign pensions and annuities (including any amounts you calculated at step 1) with a UPP. Step 4 Add up your deductible expenses. Step 5 Take amount at step 4 away from amount at step 3 and transfer to is_fsi_pension_upp. Making sure to not include as a loss any amounts by which the UPP exceeds the amount of foreign pension or annuity (including foreign tax added).
**Earliest Conditions**: For 1997-98, this variable refers to income from taxable foreign pension or annuity with an undeducted purchase price. Most foreign pensions and annuities are taxable in Australia, even if tax was withheld from your payment by the country from which the payment came. Taxpayer may claim a foreign income tax offset at this item if: - the country from which their foreign pension or annuity came withheld tax from payment ; - they were not entitled to seek a refund of the foreign tax from that country and ; - the foreign pension or annuity is also taxable in Australia.

**Form**: Individual Tax Return
**Section**: Supplementary section: Tax offsets
**Question**: Entrepreneurs tax offset
**Label**: Net small business entity income
**General Notes**: Net small business entity income amount reported by the taxpayer.
**Latest or Current Conditions**: Latest year: 2011-12. This variable refers to the net small business income for a taxpayer who is eligible to claim the entrepreneurs tax offset (ETO). The entrepreneurs tax offset (ETO) is a tax offset equal to 25% of the income tax liability attributable to the net small business income of a small business entity (either as a sole trader, partnership or trust) with an aggregated turnover of $50,000 or less. This tax offset starts to phase out when the small business entity’s aggregated turnover exceeds $50,000 and ceases when the aggregated turnover reaches $75,000.
**Latest or Current Calculations**: Latest year: 2011-12. Write the amount of share of the net small business income. For a sole trader this is the total small business entity turnover net allowable deductions.
**Earliest Conditions**: For 2005-06, this variable refers to the net income calculated under the simplified tax system (STS) for a taxpayer who is eligible for the entrepreneurs tax offset. The entrepreneurs tax offset (ETO) is a tax offset equal to 25% of the income tax liability attributable to the net STS income of a small business entity (either as a sole trader, partnership or trust) with an annual STS group turnover under a threshold.

**General Notes**: Amount of allowable franking credits that the taxpayer is entitled to claim as a franking tax offset through a partnership or a trust (see i_div_frank for definition of dividends and franking credit).
**Latest or Current Conditions**: This variable refers to the amount of allowable franking credits that the taxpayer is entitled to claim as a franking tax offset from partnership or trust (see i_div_frank for definition of dividends and franking credit) distribution. Taxpayer can only claim a share of an imputation credit which relates to the share of a franked dividend paid to a partnership or trust which is indirectly included in the amount of non-primary production partnership income or loss pt_is_pship_dist_npp), or in the amount of trust income from non-primary production (pt_is_trust_dist_npp) or non-primary production franked distribution from trusts (pt_is_frank_dist). Therefore, they cannot claim an imputation credit for a dividend paid to the partnership or trust which was an exempt distribution because family trust distribution tax or ultimate beneficiary non-disclosure tax was paid on it. They cannot claim a share of an imputation credit through a trust in the following circumstances: - the trust has an overall loss for the income year - did not show an amount of trust income from non-primary production (pt_is_trust_dist_npp) - the amount of trust income from non-primary production (pt_is_trust_dist_npp) is not attributable to the franked dividend which has generated the imputation credit. To claim a share of imputation credit in relation to the share of a franked dividend, the taxpayer must also be a ‘Qualified person’ by meeting the holding period rule and related payments rule. Division 293 tax, started in income year 2013, is an additional tax on super contributions which reduces the tax concession for individuals whose combined income and contributions are greater than the Division 293 threshold. From 1 July 2017, the threshold at which a Division 293 tax calculation will result in an assessment being issued is $250,000. For 1 July 2012 to 30 June 2017, the threshold is $300,000. Division 293 tax is payable on the excess over the threshold, or on the Division 293 super contributions, whichever is less. The rate of Division 293 tax is 15%. Division 293 super contributions equal an individual’s concessional contributions minus any excess concessional contributions. The concessional contributions counted for Division 293 tax purposes generally include: - Employer contributed amounts - Other family and friend contributions - Assessable foreign fund amounts - Assessable amounts transferred from reserves - Personal contributions for which you have been allowed a deduction - Defined benefit contributions. These contributions are concessionally taxed at 15% within the super fund. Concessional contributions in excess of the cap will be taxed at your marginal rate and Division 293 tax does not apply.

super contributions which reduces the tax concession for individuals
whose combined income and contributions are greater than the Division
293 threshold.

From 1 July 2017, the threshold at which a Division 293 tax calculation
will result in an assessment being issued is $250,000. For 1 July 2012
to 30 June 2017, the threshold is $300,000.

Division 293 tax is payable on the excess over the threshold, or on the
Division 293 super contributions, whichever is less. The rate of
Division 293 tax is 15%.

Division 293 super contributions equal an individual’s concessional
contributions minus any excess concessional contributions. The
concessional contributions counted for Division 293 tax purposes
generally include:

- Employer contributed amounts
- Other family and friend contributions
- Assessable foreign fund amounts
- Assessable amounts transferred from reserves
- Personal contributions for which you have been allowed a deduction
- Defined benefit contributions.

These contributions are concessionally taxed at 15% within the super
fund. Concessional contributions in excess of the cap will be taxed at
your marginal rate and Division 293 tax does not apply.

**Form**: Individual Tax Return

**Label**: Early repayments withdrawn from farm management deposit scheme due to natural disasters and drought
**General Notes**: Total amount of early repayments withdrawn by the taxpayer which qualifies for the natural disaster and drought assistance exemption.
**Latest or Current Conditions**: This variable refers to eligible early repayments withdrawn from farm management scheme due to natural disaster and drought. This amount is deducted from total deductible deposits and is used to calculate farm management deposit (FMD) tax concession. The taxpayer may be eligible for the farm management deposit tax concession if they received a distribution of income as a beneficiary of a trust that carried on a business of primary production. The FMD holder may be eligible to access their deposits early, without losing their concessional tax treatment, if they are eligible to claim the natural disaster assistance exception. That is if: - they made the original deposit before a natural disaster declaration was made - their primary production business received Natural Disaster Relief and Recovery Arrangements (NDRRA) Category C assistance, and - they withdrew the FMD deposit early, after they received the NDRRA Category C assistance. They may also be eligible for the drought exception. That is if: - for six consecutive months an area of their primary production property has been affected by rainfall that is within the lowest 5% of recorded rainfall for that area of their property - publicly available rainfall records held by the Bureau of Meteorology confirm this low rainfall for the period of six consecutive months preceding the month in which the repayment is made, - and for that six month period they held the deposit and were not involved solely in primary production industries like fishing, pearling, tree felling or tree transporting. Repayments of previously deducted deposits are included as assessable income in the income year they are repaid. This does not include any repayments that were reinvested, extended or transferred if they are the caretaker of a deceased estate under certain conditions.
**Latest or Current Calculations**: Add up early repayments withdrawn during the year that qualify for the natural disaster or drought exception.
**Earliest Conditions**: For 2011-12, this variable refers to eligible early repayments withdrawn from farm management scheme due to natural disaster. That is if: - they made the original deposit before a natural disaster declaration was made - their primary production business received Natural Disaster Relief and Recovery Arrangements (NDRRA) Category C assistance, and - they withdrew the FMD deposit early, after they received the NDRRA Category C assistance. Repayments of previously deducted deposits are included as assessable income in the income year they are repaid. This does not include any repayments that were reinvested, extended or transferred of if they are the caretaker of a deceased estate under certain conditions.

### is_psi_net
**Form**: Individual Tax Return
**Section**: Supplementary section: Income
**Question**: Personal service income (PSI): Net PSI - transferred from A item P1 on page 12
**Label**: Net personal service income (PSI) as a sole trader
**General Notes**: Net amount of personal services income for personal services provided as a sole trader. Those that earn PSI not as an employee may be unable to claim certain deductions relating to their PSI. This depends on whether: - they have a personal services business determination from the Commissioner of Taxation stating that your PSI was from conducting a personal services business for the whole of the period they earned PSI, or - satisfied one of the four tests outlined in Part A of the Business and professional items section in Taxpack instructions. If they meet any of the above, they do not report PSI at this question.
**Latest or Current Conditions**: This variable refers to the net PSI earned as a sole trader and as calculated in Business and professional items section A item P1: Personal service income (PSI). Personal service income is income that is mainly rewarded for an individual’s personal efforts or skills. Income can include: - personal services income under a pay as you go (PAYG) voluntary agreement - personal services income from which an amount was withheld because the Australian business number (ABN) was not quoted - personal services income from working under a labour hire arrangement as an independent contractor, payments (called specified payments) for tutorial services provided to the Indigenous Student Success Programme (formerly known as the Indigenous Tutorial Assistance Scheme) of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, translation and interpretation services provided to the Translating and Interpreting Service National of the Department of Home Affairs, or performing as a performing artist in a promotional activity, etc. It does not include income: - for supplying or selling goods, for example, from retailing, wholesaling or manufacturing - generated by an income-producing asset, for example, from operating a bulldozer - earned for granting a right to use property, for example, the copyright to a computer program - generated by a business structure, for example, a large accounting firm. Special tax treatment may apply to certain PSI as they are subject to special rules. This means that they are not able to claim certain deductions, for example rent, mortgage interest, etc, unless they satisfied the results test described in Business and professional items section (see, for example, Taxpack 2017) and received a personal services business determination(s) that was in force for the whole period of earning PSI. If they meet the above requirements, they must report their income under Business and professional items section, for example, in tax form 2017-18, it is item P8: Business income and expenses, which is then transferred to Supplementary section C item 15: Net income or loss from business (is_bus_npp).
**Latest or Current Calculations**: Transfer the amount shown at A item P1 in the Business and professional item section to is_psi_net. This amount is eligible PSI income less deductions for payments to associates for principal work and total amount of other deductions against PSI.
**Earliest Conditions**: For 2000-01, this variable refers to net personal services income earned as a sole trader including: - personal services income under a Pay As You Go (PAYG) voluntary agreement - personal services income from which an amount was withheld because Australian Business Number (ABN) was not quoted - personal services income as an independent contractor under a labour hire arrangement - personal services income from specified payments including payment for tutorial services provided for the Aboriginal Tutorial Assistance Scheme of the Department of Education, Training and Youth Affairs and payment for translation and interpretation services for the Translating and Interpreting Service of the Department of Immigration and Multicultural Affairs - other personal services income. This does not include income: - for the sale or supply of goods or granting a right to use property or - for the use of an asset. **Form**: Individual Tax Return
**Section**: Medicare levy related items
**Question**: Medicare levy reduction or exemption: Reduction based on family income - Number of dependent children and students.
**Label**: Number of dependent children or students used for calculating Medicare levy reduction.
**General Notes**: Number of dependent children or students reported by the taxpayer for the purposes of calculating the Medicare levy reduction. Pre-2003, the taxpayer also records number of dependent children or students if they are eligible for the half or full levy exemption.
**Latest or Current Conditions**: This variable refers to the number of dependent children used to calculate the family taxable income limit, which is used to determine whether or not the taxpayer is eligible for the Medicare Levy reduction. Australian residents for tax purposes are subject to a Medicare levy (for example, in 2017-18: it is 2.0% of their taxable income) unless they qualify for a reduction or exemption. A dependent child is any child who was an Australian resident whom the taxpayer maintained in the income year and whose adjusted taxable income was less than the ATI thresholds. A dependent child can be defined as either any full-time student aged under 25 years old at a school, college or university, or any child under 21 years old and was not a full time student. If the taxpayer had a spouse on 30 June of that income year or their spouse died during the income year, they must include all dependent children. If the taxpayer was single or separated on 30 June of that income year, they can only count the number of dependent children for whom they received the family tax benefit during all or part of the income year.
**Latest or Current Calculations**: Write the number of dependent children based on the above criteria.
**Earliest Conditions**: For 1990-91, this variable refers to the number of dependent children and students, which is used to determine whether the taxpayer is eligible for a Medicare levy reduction. Australian residents for tax purposes are subject to a Medicare levy of 1.25% of their taxable income above $12,528 and 20 cents for every dollar between $11,745 and $12,528. This question only applies to a taxpayer who had income greater than the threshold of $11,745 during the income year and either: (a) Had a spouse (married or de facto) on 30 June 1991 and the combined taxable income was less than $20,316 plus $2,240 for each dependent child or student. (b) Was entitled to a rebate as a sole parent or for a housekeeper or daughter-housekeeper and the taxable income was less than $20,316 plus $2,240 for each dependent child or student.

Write the number of dependent children and students.
